utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. I wanted to greet you very quickly, but I needed some patience. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Bakrac, are you ready to continue your closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom yet again. I would just like very briefly to recall since we did have a brief interruption yesterday, that before the interruption, before the adjournment yesterday, we dealt with the evidence that the Prosecution led in order to prove Simatovic's contribution to the implementation of the alleged JCE in Krajina. We have addressed the Trial Chamber, and we have indicated that there are some exhibits that strongly contradict the Prosecution's allegations. We dealt with this in part in closed session. Now I would like to say something about the testimony of a protected Prosecution witness, and therefore I would like the Trial Chamber to order the court to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I do apologise. The Prosecution has drawn the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that the Simatovic Defence devoted many pages to analysing the relationship between Captain Dragan and Franko Simatovic, and it appears to us that the Prosecution implies that the Defence had decided to set aside the Exhibit P3251 on purpose. The Defence would like to thank the Prosecution for mentioning this document, because we are convinced that this document in fact corroborates the Defence case. This is a textbook example of an intelligence document. At page 2, penultimate paragraph, Simatovic as an operative of the Belgrade centre of the State Security Service, you can see that from the heading, notes down the following words: "In the course of the interview, we have tried to provoke him," meaning Daniel Snedden, "into talking about any knowledge he might have about weapons transports through Bosnia, but he displayed no interest, refusing to discuss the topic." It is quite obvious that this is an interview between an operative and a person they were investigating. It is an attempt to use an operative method to obtain information. It is quite apparent that between the operative and the subject there is a complete lack of trust. If it is true that as early as in April 1991 at the time of that interview Simatovic and Daniel Snedden were already in close contact, if it's true that at the time Snedden was part of the plan to use him as an instructor, as a trainer for the Serb forces in the Knin Krajina area, then every reasonable trier of fact must conclude that either the plan does not exist or that Simatovic is unaware of it. This document confirms the Defence case that Franko Simatovic was involved in the effort to detect the activities of foreign intelligence services, and this includes the case of Daniel Snedden as the Defence has been claiming throughout the proceedings. Simatovic's job at the time as the member of the US section in the DB centre in Belgrade is displayed in the follow note. In the same document Simatovic says: "We believe that this case should be treated with utmost caution since all the facts indicate that Snedden has ties with the agglomerate of the Israeli, German, English, and American intelligence services." This conclusion is further corroborated by the last paragraph in this document quoted by the Prosecution where it says: "Virtually all the contacts established by Daniel Snedden may be of interest both for foreign intelligence services and for our own service. His access to the Serbian Assembly and the ministries is of particular importance." And finally Simatovic makes a proposal saying that Snedden should be brought in and interrogated about all the elements of his activities in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and his links with the foreign services and then assess the purpose and objective of further operational contacts with him. In the very last sentence, Simatovic says that the 2nd Administration and the leadership of the SDB of the Serbian Republican SUP should be consulted. So this clearly shows that in April, and this is the time when Prosecution contends the JCE began, Franko Simatovic is going about his business in the intelligence service proposing measures that include even bringing Snedden into custody. So Franko Simatovic is not the person who should arrest people. He should merely -- it was his task to submit reports about all the measures, operational measures, that he had taken. The Defence would also like to note that the Prosecution's final brief and closing arguments do not show clearly whether it is their case that Simatovic's participation in the JCE began in August 1990 with his alleged involvement in Krajina or whether his participation begins in April 1991 after the JCE has already been designed and set in motion. Regardless of which of the two arguments the Prosecution intends to pursue, the document clearly shows that by mid-April 1991, Franko Simatovic is neither aware of the alleged JCE nor is he a participant. In the oral closing arguments, the Prosecution highlighted a paragraph from Exhibit P2976 where -- well, it is a part of video recording where Captain Dragan discusses his relationship with Franko Simatovic. Captain Dragan is obviously talking about this contact in April 1991 that we have already dealt with just now. The Prosecution considers this evidence to be proof of contacts between Captain Dragan and Simatovic, but the Prosecution would also like to suggest to the Trial Chamber that at that time Captain Dragan and Simatovic were already friends. However, it is very important to read what the Exhibit P2976 actually says. In the interview, Captain Dragan says, "At that time I became sort of friends with Franko Simatovic." So when he says, "I became sort of friends with Frenki Simatovic," he is not talking about real friendship. He's talking about a relationship that can be interpreted in any number of ways. The Defence would like to reply that perhaps because of the nature of this relationship where Captain Dragan had come to realise that he was under surveillance, that he actually said this ironically. To corroborate the reasonable argument of the Defence, we can quote what Captain Dragan said at the previous page of the same exhibit where he comments on the role Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic played in Knin in the spring of 1991. Captain Dragan says the following, and it is on the previous page, and he is quite adamant about it: Frenki is an intelligence agent in that period. That segment of the service was involved in getting information from the field. Does this quote by Captain Dragan differ in any way from the Defence case that has been presented in detail in its final brief? In this case yet again the Prosecution sets aside the totality of the evidence on record and goes on to interpret the evidence piecemeal, quoting selectively, splitting the evidence artificially and using only those elements they believe can corroborate their case. Particularly striking is the Prosecution's bid to describe the relationship between Captain Dragan and the accused as very friendly on the basis of the purported warm hug between them at the awards ceremony at Kula in 1997. I will just say this: The purported warm hug in 1997 does not say anything about the relationship between Simatovic and Captain Dragan in 1991, or indeed in 1992, or at any point in time later. This hug may have been a sign of courtesy. It may have been dishonest. It may have been the result of a friendship that occurred or happened after 1996. So this hug does not tell us anything, and we don't think that it can tell anything to the Trial Chamber or be of any assistance. In its final brief, the Prosecution analysed the participation and activities of Franko Simatovic in the events in Lovinac in 1991. In the brief, the Prosecution is trying to establish a link between Simatovic and the events in Lovinac. That's in paragraphs 402 through 405. Well, first of all, Lovinac is in the immediate vicinity of a large JNA depot in Sveti Rok that had been blocked and the JNA was trying to deblock it. In the end, it deployed a very strong force and finally managed to do that. And in the course of that action, JNA took Lovinac as described in detail in our final brief in paragraphs 223 through 226. The Prosecution, however, is trying to depict the events of the 26th of September, 1991, based on D1473 to establish a link with Simatovic. At that time, he had not been in Knin for two months. The central source for this claim is Babic. The Prosecution relies on Babic's evidence about what Babic heard in Lovinac in September 1991 -- or, rather, after the events in Lovinac what he heard in a restaurant at the Knin fort. Babic testifies that he heard Simatovic boast of his participation in the event in Lovinac. That's Exhibit P1877, page 44. Witness JF-039 also testifies about Lovinac but in a completely different context. Babic figures here as the source of the claims, allegations about Simatovic as the key and central source that Prosecution is relying on. In addition to the fact that Babic's testimony is inconsistent but it is also quite vague when it comes to Simatovic. At the time when Babic testified, none of the participants was interested in Simatovic at all. Nobody tried to explain what Babic knew and what he had to say about Simatovic's role. Quite specifically, especially if we bear in mind that Babic's description of the events in Lovinac is contradicted by Mladic's entries as to who took Lovinac, what forces were used, and what the consequences were of the capture of Lovinac. And Babic's claims cannot be used to draw any conclusions about Simatovic's role in these events. In the previous proceedings, no one asked Babic what he was basing his claims on regarding Simatovic and his acts or omissions, because to put it quite simply, the participants in those proceedings were not interested. The Prosecution fails to state how many attacks there were on Lovinac. In the case file we have evidence indicating that there was fighting around Lovinac on at least three occasions in early August 1991, in early September 1991, as evidenced by Exhibit P1123, and in late September 1991 as shown by D1473. It is quite obvious that on the 16th of September, 1991, as evidenced by Exhibit P1123, Lovinac was held by the Croatian forces. All Babic's claims that Lovinac had been taken before that date, that it had been torched and looted, are simply contradicted by P1123. All claims made by JF-039 that the armoured truck -- train was used to intimidate the population and make them leave the area are likewise unfounded because the people remained in Lovinac until the 26th of September, 1991, until the attack on the JNA Colonel Trbovic. So at the time when Franko Simatovic had already been out of Krajina for a month, the Croatian population in Lovinac still remained there. Now, was anyone killed in early August in Lovinac? Did anyone leave Lovinac at that time? Were any buildings damaged on that occasion? There is simply no evidence about that in this case. The Defence would also like to highlight the issue of the armoured train and how it can be linked with Simatovic. The Prosecution makes several references to P2673, a document that is patently unauthentic. It is quite obvious that this is the case, because it bears a stamp with the Croatian chequer-board emblem. It is hard to imagine that a document that was purportedly created in Knin in June 1991 would bear such a stamp with the Croatian chequer-board. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence that one of the key causes of the unrest that erupted in Knin in the summer of 1990 was precisely the problem of the new symbols in use in Croatia, including the chequer-board. The text of the document, the dialect, the syntax clearly show that the document has nothing to do with Franko Simatovic and that he cannot be the author. The Prosecution alleges that Franko Simatovic played an important role in the events in Glina. In the context of the crimes in SAO Krajina the Prosecution mentions so-called early attacks including the attack on Glina. In paragraph 401, the Prosecution uses these arguments to show that as early as in the summer of 1991, there were attacks on the civilian population as a sort of an introduction to the events that are alleged to have happened. The Prosecution quotes P2873 where it says that about 30 houses had been destroyed. However, the same exhibit goes on to say in the very next sentence that the houses were strongly fortified and that casualties were caused because fire was opened from those houses. Exhibits P2873 and P2875 clearly indicate that fire was opened on those houses in order to neutralise legitimate military targets. The Prosecution uses P2875 to prove that this was an attack on civilian buildings, but in the very same exhibit, the author states that fire was opened at him from the civilian building. The Prosecution uses only parts of documents or in some cases just some parts of sentences in a document and the rest of the sentence that is left out by the Prosecution paint a completely different picture of the events. The evidence that is quoted by the Prosecution regarding the events in Glina cannot serve as any kind of evidence and for any kind of conclusions about the crimes that allegedly happened as early as in July 1991. And as alleged elsewhere in the Prosecution brief, they should have let the accused know what he could expect from the units he was associated with. You can see that in paragraph 747 of the final brief of the Prosecution. The Defence would like to address an event that occurred at the end of 1991. Simatovic was not in Krajina at the time, but we like to use it to illustrate how far the Prosecution is ready to go in its efforts to establish the link between Simatovic and the crimes and events that had nothing to do with him. Lacking relevant and credible evidence, the Prosecution is trying to use each and every detail to establish this link between Simatovic and the events on the ground. Another striking example is contained in paragraph 422 of the Prosecution brief where the Prosecution states that Nikola Medakovic commanded the unit of Martic's Police that attacked Saborsko, and that Medakovic trained in Golubic where he saw Simatovic as he trained there. Witnesses -- Witness Bosnic's statement is quoted in paragraph 72 of his statement. That's Exhibit D313. He says he never met Simatovic, that he heard from Medakovic that this man showed up in Golubic, that he showed up only once and that he was not involved in the training. What Medakovic told Bosnic, that he saw a man once and that he was told this was Frenki, and the fact that Medakovic took part in the attack on Saborsko several months after that conversation should serve to establish some kind of a link between Simatovic and Saborsko. The Defence considers that the manner in which the Prosecution has gone about establishing the link does not lend itself to any conclusions whatsoever. The Prosecution alleges that a person saw Simatovic at one point and that this can be used to prove that Simatovic has anything to do with Saborsko and the events there. To prove Medakovic's participation, Prosecution relies on P2628, ignoring the contents of that exhibit which gives us the full picture of who is attacking Saborsko and how. In paragraph 426 the Prosecution states that Medakovic, who saw Simatovic once in Golubic many months before, that he read out the order for the attack. However, yet again, the Prosecution is citing only a part of the sentence. It is true that Medakovic read out the order, but Medakovic did not read his own order. It was an order issued by the JNA General Bulat who commanded the attack on Saborsko, and this is all contained at page 4 of the Exhibit P2628. The exhibit also states that the JNA aircraft took part in the attack and that the JNA artillery from the Slunj training area also took part. Simatovic has nothing to do. There are no direct or indirect links between Simatovic and the attack on Saborsko. It is clear from the evidence that the Defence relies on in its brief in paragraphs 117 through 133, and it is also clear from the evidence quoted by the Prosecution if we look at them in their entirety. We used Saborsko as a striking example of a situation where Simatovic is not physically present in Krajina yet an effort is made to establish a link between him and the crimes that have nothing, nothing to do with him at all. Can we establish this link in this manner? Medakovic took part in the attack on Saborsko. Months before that, he saw Simatovic in Golubic. Thus does this establish the link? Does this prove Simatovic's responsibility for the crimes? The key witnesses and exhibits involved by the Prosecution in its brief do not give us any idea and do not constitute proof beyond reasonable doubt of the way in which Simatovic may have aided at all, let alone how he may have aided the implementation of the JCE in SAO Krajina. We would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the parts of our brief that pertain to Franko Simatovic's departure, stay, and return from the Knin Krajina. When the Defence's evidence is compared with the evidence led by the Prosecution, it becomes clear that the Prosecution has failed to prove the facts in issue regarding the events in SAO Krajina. In its written brief, the Prosecution spoke about the implementation of the JCE in Eastern Slavonia and the contribution of Franko Simatovic to that JCE. The Defence will just very briefly address some of the allegation the made by the Prosecution regarding Simatovic's role and the role of the units that are associated with him in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. In their final brief, paragraph 74 and 696, the Prosecution alleges that before the fall of Vukovar in 1991, Simatovic came to the meeting at the command of the Guards Brigade and that he also attended a ceremony to celebrate the event after the fall of Vukovar. The sole and principal evidence they rely on for this claim is the testimony of JF-033. And now, Your Honours, I would like us to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise if I was in a bit of a hurry. The Prosecution uses in their brief also some elements in the insignia of various units in 1991 through 1995. I should like to remind Your Honours that the day before yesterday, we had occasion to see a comparison between the Skorpion insignia with the emblems used by the JATD. We can also see that in paragraphs 376 through 381 of the Prosecution final brief. The Prosecution insists on a fact that is notorious and common place, that the sword is used as a symbol. I believe all the parties in the proceedings agreed on this. Page 11145. Also, the four Cyrillic letters S can be found on almost all insignia, Serbian insignia, and coat of arms. Emblems where the sword and the four letters S are together do not tell us anything about any connection between the Skorpions and the SDG or any other unit. Quite simply, those emblems were ubiquitous, and these units were used by the local authorities to provide security at oil fields. That cannot be linked to the SDB of Serbia just because one of their units also had a sword and the four letters S on their insignia. The same applies to the emblems of the Serbian Volunteers Guard. These emblems and iconography were pervasive, and this argument cannot provide a basis for making any conclusions. For the reasons stated in our final brief and as we tried to point out in our closing argument, the Prosecution has completely failed to prove any role of Franko Simatovic in the implementation of the JCE in Croatia either in the Knin Krajina or the area known as SBWS. With your leave, Your Honours, I would now give the floor to my colleague, Mr. Petrovic, who will deal with the implementation of the JCE in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I thank you for this opportunity to address you at this last stage of the proceedings against our client, Mr. Franko Simatovic. In his final trial brief, the Prosecution suggested and in his closing arguments explicitly stated that Arkan and the Volunteers Guard went to Bijeljina and Zvornik in co-ordination with Simatovic and the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. The Defence believes that the Prosecution has failed to provide any proof for such allegations. The way and the circumstances under which Arkan and the Serbian Volunteers Guard were involved in the events in Zvornik and Bijeljina have been described in detail in the Defence final brief. From that we see who invited Arkan. We see who held meetings with him, with whom -- with whose units he was in co-ordinated action, with which political structures he harmonised and agreed his activity. Simatovic is nowhere to be found in there. Regarding Bijeljina, the Defence should like to draw your attention particularly to Exhibits D84 and P1621 from which we can clearly conclude that the meeting in Bijeljina with Arkan was attended by Fikret Abdic, Biljana Plavsic, JNA General Prascevic, and JNA General Savo Jankovic, at that time commander of the JNA Tuzla Corps. At this meeting there was nobody from the DB of Serbia. The Defence particularly emphasises the testimony of the witness whom we cited in our brief in the chapter concerning Arkan and the SDG in Zvornik 1992. Defence Witness Dimitrijevic described in detail how Biljana Plavsic invited Arkan to Bijeljina, describes the co-operation between Arkan and the JNA during this operation. Transcript pages 16347 through 16349. That the testimony of Dimitrijevic was truthful and authentic is also shown by the evidence provided by the Prosecution Witness JF-025, who confirmed before this Trial Chamber that there was a meeting between Biljana Plavsic and Arkan in Bijeljina. Transcript page 6285. Biljana Plavsic herself states in Exhibit D52 that she personally directed the events in Bijeljina. From this exhibit, we clearly see the relationship and the role of Arkan and Plavsic in these events. Nobody mentions Simatovic, nor is he present at any meeting, agreement, or activity before, during, or after the fall of Bijeljina. The part of their brief that relates to Zvornik, the Prosecution begins with the heading "The accused have sent Marko Pavlovic to Zvornik." Under that heading, however, there is nothing in the text that makes it clear how exactly the accused sent that person to Zvornik. It is said that Pavlovic was a member of the DB. The cited source is the testimony of JF-026, but when we analyze that evidence, we do not find anything to confirm that Pavlovic was a member of the state security. The only thing mentioned is the connection between Pavlovic and Kostic. What exactly was the connection between Pavlovic and Kostic is something we have no information about. We also have no information about any connection between Simatovic and Kostic. So although the Prosecution suggests in the very heading that Simatovic is somehow linked with Pavlovic's arrival in Zvornik, when they try to substantiate it, they fail completely. At this point and in many other places, the Prosecution is simply trying to identify Simatovic with one entire service. The Defence have in their brief described in detail the position and the role of Simatovic in the service. Any responsibility Simatovic might bear can only be weighed in the context of his position in the service in which he worked at the relevant time. Now, Your Honours, could we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a group of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party arrived by JNA helicopter in the area of Batkusa village, JNA Colonel Nikolic decided to include these people into the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA. Colonel Nikolic is the one who issues orders to this group, as we can see from P1413. Nikolic orders this group also on the day of the killings in Crkvina. Colonel Nikolic issues orders also the day after the killings in Crkvina to the same group led by Lugar. The group that included Djordjevic and Radovanovic reports regularly on their activities to the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. We have in the case file as many as five documents showing that. However, there is absolutely no evidence that this group ever reported to the DB of Serbia. The evidence in the case file plainly shows that Djordjevic was acting on the instructions he received from the command of the JNA air force. General Bajic is involved in bringing Djordjevic to Samac. General Bajic decides whether Djordjevic should be sent back to Serbia. In December 1992, Mladic notes down Todorovic's words that he knew Colonel Jeremic and General Bajic and that it was with their mediation that he had sent men for training and that they returned to the area of Samac together with 30 volunteers from Kragujevac. We can see that in Exhibit P3117. Todorovic, according to the Mladic diaries, never mentioned the DB of Serbia or Simatovic. If Simatovic had had any important role in these events, there would be no reason for Todorovic not to mention it and no reason for Mladic not to note it. The Defence refers to our detailed arguments in paragraphs 1137 through 1213. There is a wealth of documents about these events and the players involved in the area of Samac. The totality of these documents point to the unequivocal conclusion that the events in Samac pursued a dynamic that Simatovic had no influence over. And finally, even if it were true that Simatovic was present when that group of 20 men was leaving by JNA helicopter to Samac, the events in this town involved TO and JNA units with hundreds of fighting men, machinery, artillery, organisation, and logistics which make the participation of 20 men symbolic and minor. That is the only participation that Simatovic could have, if any, in these events, minor, peripheral, and insignificant from the point of view of the course and outcome of these events. I am looking at the clock, Your Honours. Perhaps it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us where you are approximately, Mr. Petrovic, in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe we will manage to conclude within the time granted us. If my math is correct, that would be between 30 and 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with your math. We take a break. Would it be wise to take the break five minutes shorter than usual so that we are not ending up in either -- I mean, the Defences -- the two Defence are the last to use the one hour left, and I think I would be hesitant to cut it short, or, on the other hand, to rely on the voluntary co-operation of all those assisting us. They have children at home as well, which they may have to fetch and so I suggest that we take exceptionally a five-minute shorter break and we will resume at five minutes to 4.00. And that you would then finish, Mr. -- the Simatovic Defence would finish anywhere between 4.25 and 4.30. We take a break and we resume at 5 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As our closing arguments continue, I would like to address very briefly the events in Doboj, some aspects of those events, in the year 1992. In this context, the Prosecution alleges that Simatovic visited Ozren several times, and in doing so relies on the evidence of Witness JF-005. Now, in order to deal with the testimony of that witness, Your Honours, I would like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In their final brief, the Prosecution lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In their final brief, the Prosecution lists three events that should convince the Trial Chamber about the existence of the intent on Simatovic's part in relation to the events that he's charged with. These three events should provide the basis for the existence of this intent through direct reference to what he said and what he did. In this context, the Prosecution draws our attention to the events in Lovinac - we've already addressed that - in Vukovar, ditto, and the events in Eastern Bosnia in the first half of 1993. If we're talking about the events in 1993 in Eastern Bosnia, we are talking about an operation that was code named Strike, Udar. In the final brief, in the part under the heading "VRS under Mladic, VJ and Simatovic" planned and carried out operations in Eastern Bosnia in line with the JCE, paragraphs 133 through 136 of the final brief lists its conclusions regarding this operation, Operation Strike. As I've already noted, this operation is again invoked in the part of the final brief where they talk about Simatovic's intent to implement the joint criminal enterprise. The heading is Simatovic personally took part in the planning of Operation Strike and the exercise of command of the units in this operation. That's paragraph 698. The Prosecution allegations regarding Operation Strike is a very good example of how the Prosecution embarks on a fishing expedition, searching for any kind of evidence against Simatovic using fragments of evidence, interpreting them out of context, exaggerating their importance and presenting them as evidence that should create an impression of a general pattern of conduct. The Defence has dealt with Operation Strike in its final brief in paragraphs 1058 through 1059, but we would now like to respond to some of the arguments presented by the Prosecution. The very heading of the two sections of the final brief indicate that the Prosecution wants to suggest that Simatovic planned and carried out the operation hand-in-hand with Mladic and the VJ. The evidence shows that the opposite was the case. In the analysis of combat operations in Operation Strike, that's P3118, states that Operation Strike was carried out on the basis of a combat order issued by the VRS Main Staff on the 15th of February, 1993. The Drina Corps issued it's own combat order on the 12th of February, 1993, and a preliminary order issued on the 20th of February, 1993, shows that the plan for Operation Strike had been drafted before that time. All the other orders that were issued within the framework of this operation were drafted several weeks after the meeting that was allegedly attended by Simatovic, and it is very difficult to establish a link between them and the discussions at the meeting. Likewise, Exhibit P3118 specifies who controlled Operation Strike, lists all the forces that were deployed, and we can see that those forces came from the Drina Corps, and there is a separate list of the forces that were not part of the Drina Corps but took part in the operation. If we look at this exhibit, we can see that Simatovic is not there, and we cannot see any evidence of any unit that would directly or indirectly be linked with him. A detailed order of the Drina Corps for Operation Strike is dated the 12th of February, 1993, and is also on record as Exhibit P3085. This exhibit also shows when the plans were made, who made the plans, which units took part in the operation, and in what positions. Finally, Prosecution Witness Manojlo Milovanovic as the highest ranking and, indeed, the only VRS officer to testify at this trial states that he knew that Operation Strike had been planned but that it had never been carried out. I would like to refer you to transcript pages 4437 through 4438. Thus the Prosecution has in front of it an entry from Mladic's diary stating that Simatovic attended a meeting. If you look at the original of the entry, you can see that Simatovic's name was added subsequently to the entry that pertains to the 28th of February, 1993. You can see that from the way in which his name and the names of two other persons is inserted between two lines in this entry. Simatovic did not say anything at the meeting. We don't know why he came. We don't know how long he remained there. All this is immaterial for the Prosecution. The Prosecution indeed interprets Simatovic's presence there as evidence that he took part in the planning and as proof that VRS was under Simatovic's command. Evidence can be interpreted in any number of ways. It can be interpreted in various contexts, but facts that do not exist cannot become evidence that merits any kind of discussion. Evidence of Operation Strike on record is complete, including Milovanovic's testimony, which is also there. Any effort to squeeze in Simatovic in some kind of a role is not based on the evidence. Now I would like very briefly to say something about -- something that the Prosecution used as a motto of some sort for the closing chapter of its final brief. In the brief dealing with the crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Prosecution uses Seselj's statement made at the time while the war was still going on, paragraph 486 of the Prosecution's brief. At the time when he made the statement, Seselj was in political conflict with Milosevic, and everything that Seselj said at the time was fruit of his political propaganda. Seselj is on trial before this Tribunal for his actions from that time, and he is in the UN detention unit and is accessible to the Prosecution. However, the Prosecution did not call Seselj as its witness. If it really believes that Seselj credibly and truthfully describes the events, that would be the only and logical way to proceed, but the Prosecution prefers to use fragments of Seselj's political propaganda, of his tirades and the night that he made in the 1990s and wants the Trial Chamber to trust what Seselj is saying. The Prosecution quotes what Seselj has said in a documentary series, "The Death of Yugoslavia," six times. Not only does the Prosecution quote Seselj, Seselj's words are used as a motto of a whole chapter in the Prosecution brief, and this chapter contains 43 pages. The Prosecution objected to Seselj's statements being admitted into the case file, and we still believe that Seselj's statement from the 1990s cannot be used as a basis for any relevant conclusions in the context of this case. Seselj wrote hundreds of books, many of them while in detention, and many claims he made in those books are questionable, to say the least, in terms of their reliability and truthfulness and cannot be used in these proceedings or indeed any other proceedings. Now I would like us to move into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Petrovic, I think you referred us to paragraphs 1058 and 1059 for Operation Udar, Operation Strike. Now, I do not find even one reference in those paragraphs in your final brief, because that's what we're talking about, isn't it? It is -- the heading is "Simatovic in Bajina Basta," and that's before 1057, and then we move to 1058 and 1059.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours. Let me just have a look. As we respond to the Prosecution's arguments, I will use one sentence to explain that. It may have been a typo or something like that. I don't have it now.

utterances.text: Yes. We're trying to -- to find all the references you're making. If you could assist us at a later stage that's appreciated. Please proceed. And I think you wanted us --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You wanted us to turn into private session. And we are close to the time, well, let's say five to eight minutes where you're supposed to conclude. Please proceed. If I said five to eight, that's perhaps -- it is, I would say 8 to 12. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now I would like to say a few words about the so-called payroll lists. There are dozens of JATD payroll lists in the case file in this case, and out of all of those payroll lists only five are signed by Simatovic. In each of these documents, it is clearly stated that Simatovic signed them for deputy commander Milan Radonjic. Had Simatovic really been the JATD commander, as the Prosecution alleges, there is no reason why he would want to conceal this fact in an internal document of the service in 1994 and 1995. It is a notorious fact that a commander would not sign a document instead of his deputy using the formula "for" in the signature block. Finally, we would like to conclude our closing argument by saying this: All the arguments presented today in court and yesterday in court and in our final brief paint a clear picture of the position and role that Simatovic had in the relevant time in light of the indictment. The Prosecution is trying to prove -- or to prove that Simatovic had discriminatory intent, trying to portray Simatovic as a man fighting for a Greater Serbia without other nations and peoples, as a man who destroys and expels all those who are not Serb. The Prosecution is trying to attribute this to a man whose family has deep rots in Croatia, whose relatives lived in Croatia during the war and who still live there. The Prosecution is trying to attribute this to Simatovic, a man who never said or did anything against any other man, other state, or other nation. Every action Simatovic took was taken in line with the rules of the service that he belonged to with the laws and the constitution of the country in which he lived. Simatovic was an intelligence agent, and intelligence work requires people to go abroad, calls for contacts with all sorts of people. You have to be close to the events. You have to establish your intelligence contacts and networks. All these activities are defined by the rules of the service and Simatovic never deviated from them. Simatovic did not commit a single crime. Simatovic did not aid in the commission of a single crime. Your Honours, the Defence is convinced that there's every reason for this Trial Chamber to acquit Simatovic and believes that the Trial Chamber will do so once it has looked at all the arguments presented by the Defence in the final brief and in our closing arguments. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Before we continue, could I ask to go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Maxine Marcus will present the Prosecution's submissions in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it has been scheduled for one hour. I would say that you use 45 minutes, that we then take a break, and then you reserve your last 15 minutes for after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will be very strict on time, so I appreciate that you do your best Ms. Marcus, but it's the result that counts primarily. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon. This afternoon I will correct some misrepresentations made by Defence counsel during their closing submissions. I will correct their submissions on matters of corroboration. I will challenge their closing assertions regarding the Kula ceremony and the evidence of JF-039. I will correct their closing misrepresentations regarding the evidence of the relationships between key JCE members and the accused. I will respond to their ineffective attempt, yet again, to challenge the sufficiency of the pleadings, and finally I will respond to their submissions regarding mens rea. I also have a few slides to accompany my submissions. The Stanisic Defence argues at transcript 20298 that intercept P671 is obviously a forgery because the audio of that intercept does not exist. The Prosecution seeks to remind Your Honours that the Chamber has admitted the corresponding monitor note as P716 which is a contemporaneous record that the monitors prepared at the time that the conversation was recorded. The monitor note appears on the same page as another admitted intercept, P670, for which the audio does exist, and the content of which is consistent with and related to the content of P671. This demonstrates the authenticity of the monitor note and attests to the reliability of the intercept. At transcript 20290 to -91, the Stanisic Defence argue that according to JF-032, Bogunovic should have been at the meeting in Dalj with Stanisic, but that Bogunovic did not confirm that evidence. Upon review of the evidence, however, it is clear that JF-032 never said that Bogunovic was there. JF-032 testified that a policeman named Borislav Bogdanovic was one of the police officers who were with him when Stanisic arrived. That's at transcript 4757. When the Stanisic Defence later suggested to JF-032 in cross-examination that Borislav Bogunovic had been there, his answer was that he did not remember Minister Bogunovic being present. That's at transcript 4760. I also refer Your Honours to transcript page 4758 where the Prosecution pointed out to Defence counsel that the witness had spoken about a Bogdanovic and not a Bogunovic and he acknowledged and accepted this correction. I will now discuss the matter of corroboration raised by the Defence in their closing. The Stanisic Defence has argued that the Prosecution relies on the Mladic notebooks without corroboration which "is likely to create the conditions for a miscarriage of justice." That's at page 20271. The Mladic notebooks are not a special class of evidence that require special corroboration but must be individually weighed and assessed by the Chamber like all evidence. I refer the Chamber to its decision admitting the notebooks on the 10th of March, 2011, which declines to require corroboration for admission and sets forth several factors showing the notebooks to be reliable. On slide 26 of their closing arguments, the Defence cited to the Prosecution's statement on the 21st of March of 2012 that the Prosecution had tendered only portions of the notebooks that we believed to be corroborated by other evidence before the Chamber. The Prosecution's argument regarding the reliability of the excerpts that we tendered did not create a new higher burden for these pieces of evidence. Can I please have slide 2. Regardless, the Mladic notebooks are well corroborated and slide 2 sets forth some of the corroborating evidence for the first three items challenged by the Defence's slide 28 as examples. Stanisic takes an extremely narrow view of the meaning of corroborative evidence both in the context of the Mladic notebooks where corroboration is not specially required as well as in the context of 92 quater evidence. Taking the first example on slide 2, P3215 and P3216 are excerpts from notebooks from the latter half of 1991. They are cited in the brief for the proposition that Mladic had the number for Golubic from 1991. The notebooks are corroborated by other evidence of phone numbers that match the phone numbers in the Mladic notebooks and by other evidence that Golubic was relevant to Mladic at the time. Obviously neither of those pieces of corroborating evidence would be cited in our brief for the fact that Mladic had the Golubic phone number, but the corroborative evidence makes this fact all the more reliable. Slide 28 of the Defence closing lists 18 examples of propositions in the Prosecution's brief that cite exclusively to the Mladic notebooks. This same analysis I have just done can also be done for each of those examples, and in many cases the corroboration is found in the same or in adjacent paragraphs. Slide 3, please. On the matter of corroboration of 92 quater evidence, I refer the Chamber to the decision on appeal against the Martic's Trial Chamber's decision on the evidence of Witness Milan Babic. That is dated the 14th of September, 2006, in paragraph 22 which states: "Evidence which has not been cross-examined and goes to the acts and conduct of the accused or is pivotal to the Prosecution case will require corroboration if used to establish a conviction." I note for the Chamber also the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Prlic case dated 23 November 2007 at paragraph 59. I will now turn to the corroboration of JF-039. Throughout their submissions yesterday and today both Defence teams claimed that the Prosecution is asking the Chamber to take a partial view of the evidence. In fact, it is the Defence that wishes Your Honours to take a partial view of the evidence, particularly when it comes to the corroboration of Prosecution witnesses. JF-039 is very solidly corroborated. For example, we heard a lot yesterday about how laughable was JF-039's testimony about the close relationship between Stanisic and Martic. But Your Honours, Jovica Stanisic's name is the first name on P428, a list of persons receiving awards from the RSK MUP for demonstrated bravery, self-sacrifice, or exceptional contribution to the RSK internal affairs services. C-015 testified that Martic referred to Stanisic as his "only and first commander" at transcript 1624. Other exhibits such as P995, P12, and P2667 also corroborate JF-039 on this point. If the Chamber takes the Defence at their word and views the evidence as a whole, it will find that JF-039 is well corroborated by independent evidence. We don't have time today to go into every aspect of JF-039's evidence but he is equally well corroborated on other points. For example, his evidence about the relationship between the DB and Captain Dragan is corroborated by P61, P3251, P1069, P1186, and P2976 as well as other evidence. He is also corroborated by Babic. Babic and JF-039 viewed events from their respective positions, and their opportunities to observe events and people varied as well; yet they are remarkably consistent. Even the supposed contradiction between Babic and JF-039 yesterday asserting that Babic was completely unaware of arrangements between Martic and Stanisic prior to March 1991 is inaccurate. That's at page 20274 and -75. Babic was certainly aware that Martic and Stanisic were meeting together in August 1990, because Babic met Martic and Stanisic together at a cafe between Knin and Golubic at that time. That's P1877, pages 96 to 98, and pages 56 to 59. I'm sorry. The second page refers to Exhibit P1878, pages 56 through 59. He also knew that Martic received weapons and the Knin police station distributed weapons from August 1990. He testified that some of the same people who brought weapons to Martic in 1990 later distributed weapons they had obtained through Stanisic. That's P1878 at page 40 and page 149. Moreover, Babic's testimony reveals that when he met Milosevic in March of 1991, it became apparent that Milosevic, Bogdanovic, and Stanisic had already been involved in sending weapons to the Krajina without Babic's knowledge. Bogdanovic told him, You don't have to know everything. That's P1878, pages 153 to 154. JF-039's and Babic's different levels of knowledge about these events simply reflects their different positions and different relationships. It is certainly not evidence of perjury. I will now respond to submissions made regarding the Kula ceremony. Slide 4, please. Your Honours, the Defence continue to maintain that the Kula award ceremony was an elaborate ruse intended to impress Milosevic. This argument is nonsense as is clearly shown by the fact that the ceremony continued after Milosevic left. At 41 minutes and 42 seconds of P61, Milosevic gets into a large black Mercedes and drives off. What happens after that? There are no congratulations to each other at the performance for Milosevic. The ceremony continues as before with perhaps a bit less formality. Stanisic gives Captain Dragan an award and he says he is proud to present it. He and Simatovic both embrace Captain Dragan. Opacic salutes Stanisic, who then gives him an award. Stanisic then gives a brief speech recognising Opacic for his heroism in the Knin area and also another member from the Banija area. Your Honours, Milosevic is gone. Nothing that is happening at this point in the ceremony could possibly be for his benefit or to impress him. Nevertheless, what happens after Milosevic leaves is completely consistent with what happened while he was there. We heard Defence counsel yesterday at page 20299 attempt to dismiss the accused's embrace of Captain Dragan by paraphrasing Frank Sinatra: A kiss is but a kiss. A hug is but a hug. It was a clever device designed, no doubt, to diminish with honour the significance of this event -- of this evidence, but when Stanisic warmly embraces a man whose activities and intentions he claims to have been suspicious of, when Simatovic warmly embraces a man he claims he never had any contacts with, a hug is not just a hug. Your Honours, the next part of my submission will discuss the relationship between the accused and key JCE members. Slide 5, please. I will start with the relationship between Stanisic and Karadzic. The Stanisic Defence seemed to suggest yesterday that the Prosecution's case about the relationship between Karadzic and Stanisic rested entirely on intercepted conversations from before the war. This ignores Exhibit P2532, the record of the meeting in Belgrade in December 1993 at which Stanisic asks Karadzic how Serbia could help him and Karadzic then evaluated the progress of the war in terms of the six strategic goals. And, Your Honours, despite the Defence's repeated arguments that Mladic was somehow attempting to incriminate Stanisic with his notebooks, the fact is this meeting really occurred. Your Honours heard evidence from someone who attended it. General Milovanovic confirmed that this meeting occurred and confirmed the details of this notebook entry in some detail at transcript pages 15445 to 15448. It's because of Milovanovic that we know that the meeting took place at the DB building. Simatovic also unconvincingly attempts to minimise his relationship with Karadzic. They emphasise that P693 is the only recorded conversation between Simatovic and Karadzic and they ask Your Honours to conclude based on that that it was not a close relationship. That's at transcript 20323. But this intercept shows that Simatovic and Karadzic knew each other, had close personal regard for each other, and viewed themselves as being engaged in a common project. I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 115 to 117 of our final brief and transcript page 11055 for more on this intercept. Similarly, the Simatovic Defence takes an unduly restrictive view of the relationship between Mladic and Simatovic, emphasising that there is evidence of them attending just two meetings together. This argument also made today at transcript -- temporary transcript page 31 ignores the importance of one of those meetings, the one regarding Operation Udar recorded in P392. That meeting was attended by the top leadership of the VJ and the VRS and concerned a major military operation in Eastern Bosnia that was part of a larger VRS plan to drive out the Muslim population from that region as set out in the third strategic goal. I refer the Chamber to paragraphs 133 to 137 of our brief. The fact that Mladic and Simatovic attended this meeting together clearly shows that they shared this common goal. I would note that the participation of Simatovic and the Red Berets in this operation is established by the evidence that I cited in slide 2 of the rebuttal slides. Simatovic has made several attempts to deny responsibility for crimes, arguing that he was not physically present, first in the Krajina, yesterday first at 20325 to -6, and then today at temporary transcript page 15. As the Chamber noted in its decision to admit Simatovic's passport on the 5th of July, 2012: "The Prosecutor does allege that the accused physically and personally committed any of the crimes he has been charged with. In other words, it is not necessary for the accused to have been physically present in the region where the crimes were committed in order to be criminally responsible for them." A few words about the Simatovic Defence claims in their submissions today. In their final brief, the Simatovic Defence stated: "The foregoing evidence shows clearly and beyond doubt that Daniel Snedden, aka Captain Dragan, had no contacts or connections with the Serbian DB." That is paragraph 295. During their submissions today, they appear to accept that Simatovic did meet with Captain Dragan in April 1991 as outlined in P3251. Of the meeting, they said it is "quite obvious that this is an interview between an operative and a person they were investigating." That is today's transcript at page 6. What they did not explain is how a claim of no contact or connections between Dragan and Simatovic is consistent with an obvious record of an interview between Captain Dragan and Simatovic. They also claimed that we were selectively quoting Captain Dragan's words in P2976, the unit video, and that Captain Dragan was probably being ironic when he described his relationship with Simatovic as a kind of friendship. According to the Defence, "he's talking about a relationship that can be interpreted in way number of ways." That was today's transcript at page 8. I would just remind Your Honours of another thing that Dragan says in P2976. He says: "The unit existed at all times formally or informally, whether with 15 people in it or 300 at the end. I commanded the unit in one period, Frenki in another, Legija in yet another, but the unit existed at all times." That's P2976 at page 17. Your Honours, this is not a relationship that can be interpreted in any number of ways. Simatovic and Dragan co-operated in the establishment, training, and command of a special unit. Regarding P2673, the armour train document. The Defence's arguments are strained and unpersuasive. They rely first on the language claiming that the document is written in the Ijekavian dialect which Simatovic would not have used. Leaving aside the question of whether that is accurate or not, Simatovic could certainly have approved and signed the document without having typed every word himself; arguably, that would be nor likely. The Simatovic Defence also rely on the stamp of P2673 in which they see a chequer-board. While one Simatovic Defence witness, DFS-14, described the stamp as containing a chequer-board, a Stanisic Defence witness gave what we submit is far more accurate evidence about the smudge at the bottom of the page. When asked by the Simatovic Defence whether he saw a chequer-board in the stamp, Witness Mile Bosnic said, "You mean these blots here?" He then says, "I can't make out anything at all." That's at transcript page 12879. These blots are no basis on which to dismiss the document. Your Honours, a few words about notice. Slide 6, please. This particular challenge to the sufficiency of the pleadings in this case which is raised by the Stanisic Defence in their final trial brief and now in their closing submissions was already sensibly decided by the Pre-Trial Chamber in this case in 2003 and in 2006. Although the Defence tried to reargue this matter of the sufficiency of the pleadings in 2009 and again in 2012, all motions on this particular matter were denied or deemed to have been already fully litigated. The Defence argued in 2003 that the allegations against the accused in the first indictment suggest they were sufficiently proximate to the underlying crimes in the instant case so as to oblige the Prosecution to list in the indictment all the names of the members of the groups in the indictment. The Pre-Trial Chamber rejected that argument stating: "Neither Stanisic nor Simatovic are alleged to have physically committed the crimes charged personally." They are charged with comission through a JCE and other modes of liability. The names of the members of the group were held to be evidence and not material facts and the first indictment was found to be sufficiently specific on the matter of the inclusion of groups rather than names. I refer Your Honours to the decision on the Defence preliminary motions of 14 November 2003, pages 3 to 4. The Defence did not seek certification to appeal. In 2006, when the Defence challenged the sufficiency of the Trnovo charges in the Second Amended Indictment asserting, inter alia, that the individual identities of the Bosnian Serb forces who handed over the Trnovo victims to the Skorpions are material facts. They were denied on this issue on the same grounds, that the names are a matter of evidence. That was on the 12th of April, 2006. The Defence did not seek certification to appeal that decision. In 2009 when the Defence filed and untimely challenge to the sufficiency of the third amended indictment, inter alia, on the pleading of physical perpetrators that motion was denied for lack of good cause for its untimeliness. Their motion was filed on the 2nd of November, 2009. The Defence did not seek certification to appeal that decision. In their 2012 motion for exclusion of this evidence, inter alia, on the grounds that the indictment was not sufficiently specific, the Chamber held that the form of the indictment matter had already been fully litigated. That's a decision of this Chamber on the 15th of August, 2012, at paragraph 11. Certification to appeal that decision was denied. The Pre-Trial Chamber's decisions in 2003 and 2006 on this issue were correct according to the jurisprudence. It is well established, Your Honours, that an indictment is required to plead the material facts upon which the Prosecution relies but not the evidence by which those material facts are to be proved. I refer Your Honours to the Furundzija Appeal Judgement, paragraph 147, the Kupreskic Appeal Judgement, paragraph 88, and the Kvocka Appeal Judgement, paragraph 27. According to the Kvocka Appeal Judgement in paragraph 28 and the Kupreskic Appeal Judgement in paragraph 89 the materiality of a particular fact depends upon: "The Prosecution's characterisation of the alleged criminal conduct and the proximity of the accused to the underlying crime." The 2003 and 2006 decisions of the Pre-Trial Chamber in this case found the pleadings to be sufficient. They found the names of physical perpetrators to be a matter of evidence, not material facts. They did not rest their decisions on the facts of other cases raised by the Defence in their submissions. They rests their decisions on the facts of this case. Prior decisions on this ground have thus failed and their last-minute attempt in their closing submissions to persuade the Chamber to reconsider these decisions should also fail. At transcript page 38 today, the Simatovic Defence claimed: "It is a notorious fact that a commander would not sign a document instead of his deputy using the formula 'for' in the signature block," attempting to downplay the significance of Simatovic's signature on the payment lists. Defence Witness Micic testified that this was not the case, that in the DB, he "always put the word 'za,'" meaning "for," "whether it was my superior or my subordinate that I was signing for." That's at transcript 19868. A few final responsive words about mens rea, Your Honours. May I please request private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Stanisic Defence spent many words yesterday trying to demonstrate that Mr. Stanisic's actions show that he did not have the intent to commit the charged crimes. The Stanisic Defence seeks to present Mr. Stanisic as a peacemaker. If only it had been, as asserted by the Stanisic Defence, the intent of Mr. Stanisic to "be in contact with the leadership to advance peace," to engage in "quiet diplomacy," and to "ameliorate the pain and suffering." If only his intent had not been criminal. Just imagine of if a man of that character, influence, and fame, as cited by the Stanisic Defence in their brief at paragraph 1261, would have exerted this influence not only to protect the expatriate UN hostages but to protect the Bosniak, Trnovo, and Sanski Most victims. Imagine how history could have been different. The fact is that the accused continued to support Arkan and the Skorpions in their murderous acts during precisely the same time period as the hostage crisis. That is because, we assert, the killing of the expatriate hostages would not have furthered the common criminal plan. It would likely have blocked it. The ill gotten gains of the criminal plan could only be made permanent through a peace plan that recognised them. Peace negotiations were an integral part of the plan and not evidence that no plan existed. Thank you.
