utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, the differences in approach taken by the Prosecution and the Stanisic Defence with regard to this case may be summed up in a very simple phrase: Assertion versus evidence. Taking as our starting point the Prosecution's closing on Tuesday, that is the theme of this reply. As we noted yesterday, we, the Defence, believe we have addressed all the salient evidence in our final brief and in our closing remarks of yesterday. We have sought to address each and every piece, good or bad, and offered reasonable explanations that stand as a rebuttal of the Prosecution case on the vital issues. As we noted yesterday, Stanisic's proximity to the events, and I would add to that the misbehaviour of some of those with relationships to the DB, mean that it is not possible to remove all the suspicion, but we do not have to. That is not sufficient to convict Mr. Stanisic. So we once again urge Your Honours to examine the Prosecution and Defence submissions with a critical eye, as we know Your Honours will, to ascertain whether an assertion giving rise to suspicion has been transformed by evidence into proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Unfortunately, in a case this voluminous and complex, that distinction may be easily blurred, especially in the hands of a skilful and determined Prosecution. The difference is critical in this trial with regard to the issues of the special units, especially the alleged Red Beret unit that Stanisic is alleged to have created at Golubic and is said to have been continuous throughout the indictment period. The case of that alleged continuous unit revolves around both Prosecution and Defence assertions. We urge you to find both insufficient and look carefully at the evidence. This is vital if the law is to be respected, especially concerning joint criminal enterprise and the tools test. If I may just explain why we take that view. The Prosecution relies upon a volume of statement within personnel files wherein men claim they were in a unit since May 1991. The Prosecution claim they are entitled to adduce any number of new direct perpetrators at any time without consequence, and further to allow the Defence to assert as we have that they are direct perpetrators and without illuminating Your Honours as to whether that's correct, and to allow Your Honours to rule that the Defence have been speculative without correcting that position. Only now are the Prosecution willing to confirm that these men are relied upon as direct perpetrators. We leave that matter for Your Honours and for Your Honours to consider whether drip feeding direct perpetrators into a trial is sufficient and whether that undermines the Defence's right to the preparation of an effective defence. What the Pre-Trial Chamber said or what Your Honours said at the beginning of trial before the drip feeding of these direct perpetrators into the trial is one thing, another thing is what Your Honours will need to decide when looking at that issue now at the end of a long and complex trial. Putting aside that issue, what these men claim in these personnel files are assertions only, assertions that we are not able to test because the evidence came late but also because none of these men have been called to allow them to be cross-examined. As I said, the Defence also relies upon witnesses who make assertions. The Prosecution evidence contained in P973 at page 7 about a man who met Simatovic on Tara who gained the impression that the men around him were more of a group than a unit, that same evidence confirming that Simatovic was engaged in founding a new unit, not the formalising of an old one. Sliskovic, his first account, where he told the Prosecution that he understood that a Serbian DB unit was being re-established. JF-048 also confirmed again in his first account that men who applied to join the JATD in 1993 applied to join a new unit. As he confirmed towards the latter part of his senior year, representatives of the so-called Red Berets came to his school to see if anyone was interested in joining. I made an error there. It's not 1993, it's April of 1995. He noted, and I quote, "This unit was relatively new." He testified that he was told that the roots of the unit went back to the Alpha camp, I quote, "That our first instructors were trained there." Your Honours will see that at P523, pages 3 to 4. In other words, what he said before being proofed by the Prosecution in this case was that the instructors had been trained at the Alpha training camp, which as Your Honours will see from the exhibits such as P3061, opened in 1993, but in April 1995, this unit was relatively new. Your Honours will note that we rely upon the Prosecution evidence in the main for these assertions. We also rely upon Krsmanovic, who despite the obvious logic that he must have known on the Prosecution case that infamous men such as Bozovic had been pivotal to this unit since 1991, asserted in this court that the unit being created was new, and he acted accordingly. We have the evidence. He applied for operative checks for all these men, including Bozovic. So we have contradictory assertions. We know that. Where does that take us? Well, it takes Your Honour, with respect, to the applicable law and the evidence in support. That's how we can resolve this contradiction in the assertions, and the applicable law is the tools test, and the evidence is what the Prosecution has proven happened on the ground. Self-serving claims in personnel files cannot satisfied the test. The type of criteria that must be addressed by the evidence before Mr. Stanisic may be found responsible for members of a unit acting in furtherance of crime and the Prosecution's criminal purpose was summed up by the Appeals Chamber who adopted the approach from the Krajisnik case, and I refer Your Honours to slide 1 which is on the screen. Slide 1 sums up the kind of evidence which would distinguish perpetrators of crimes acting as part of a joint criminal enterprise from persons not part of that joint criminal enterprise but who were committing similar crimes. That is the problem with the Prosecution's approach to notice in this trial. It not only prejudices the accused, but it also undermines their case. In the main, Your Honours have not been told what these men did other than they were in a unit, nor has the Prosecution adduced except in a handful of cases which we address in depth in our brief what crimes they committed, whether the perpetrators' act advanced the objective of the joint criminal enterprise, whether members of the joint criminal enterprise ratified the perpetrators' act implicitly or explicitly, and so on and so forth. More basically, the Prosecution have not defined for each phrase -- phase of the indictment or particular event the unit's command structure. They haven't identified briefings attended by the men, any rules of the organisation, any orders or instructions in relation to most of the men except they assert Stanisic and Simatovic were in command. It is plainly not sufficient to point to assertions of the existence of a unit and then request that Your Honours presume on the basis of a handful of men's conduct that it existed and acted in furtherance of crime at the behest of Mr. Stanisic. A gushing award ceremony after the fact does not resolve these evidential problems. Whether Milosevic was present or not, there was a number of dignitaries who remained after Milosevic left. Do the Prosecution suggest that the DB having engaged in such a charade should have just shut up shop and gone home? In any event, it isn't enough. It's an assertion and nothing more. The Prosecution's approach in this case in relation to these types of assertions is compounded by inaccurate assertions by the Prosecution in their brief and an attempt as we indicated yesterday to reverse the burden of proof. Slides 2, 3, and 4 are representative samples respectively. Let me add one other assertion which we heard today from the Prosecution. C-015 testified that Martic referred to Stanisic as his only and first commander. Assertion. It doesn't corroborate JF-039. It's an assertion devoid of evidential support. If C-015 had offered a scintilla of support for the alleged weapon supplies, then we might be able to talk about corroboration and we might be able to talk about evidence and not assertion. Slide 5 sums up aspects of the Prosecution oral closing that we want to deal with in this reply. We shall follow the structure Your Honours see on the screen. We shall once again demonstrate that the Prosecution's approach remains limited to proffering assertions, not evidence, and unreliable assertions at that. Slide 6. The Prosecution allege at transcript 20181, that the relationship between the accused was a close relationship of co-operation and trust during the indictment period. It is the most important relationship among JCE members in this case. Slide 6 enumerates the evidence that the Prosecution alleges amounts to tremendous support for this thesis. As we can see, it exists or it amounts to witnesses' impressions. It is also, as Your Honours can see, limited to the three witnesses whose evidence relates to 1991 in the main. Assertion, not evidence. We submit each salient event or alleged use of direct perpetrators must be looked at on a case-by-case basis to see what Stanisic's relationship to Simatovic was at that time. Whether the evidence shows Stanisic was involved and whether he procured Simatovic, this on a case-by-case basis. Slide 7, the relationship between Stanisic and Badza. Slide 7 sums up the one piece of evidence that the Prosecution relies upon to support this gargantuan assertion that Stanisic was Badza's boss. Milovanovic did not confirm that Badza had indicated Stanisic was his boss, and even if he had, to rest a whole relationship for five years on such an assertion would be wholly wrong. Slide 8 and slide 9 addresses the Prosecution's submissions concerning the irrelevance of tension between Milosevic, Karadzic, and Krajisnik. The Prosecution relies upon the evidence of Sir Ivor Roberts to suggest that these conflicts did not extend to the DB. Once again, the Prosecution rely upon an assertion Sir Ivor Roberts uttered. I quote: "That was the impression one had for the reasons I was saying earlier, that while the political leadership were very much out of sympathy with each other. At other levels, conversations and understandings continued between state security people and the armies. First of all, the Prosecution appear to misunderstand our submission. We are not only arguing that the Bosnian Serbs were not pursuing a criminal purpose during 1995, we are also submitting that even if they were, the Belgrade leadership were no longer part of that enterprise. Further, if one looks at what Sir Ivor Roberts says, he says that he had the impression that conversations and understandings continued between the state security people. That's a long way away from concerted action and furtherance of crime. Slide 8, which you have on your screen, confirms the dangers of relying on impressions. It shows some of the evidence that shows not only was the Serbian DB alone in not co-operating with the Bosnian Serb DB, but by the time 1995 came, any minimal relationship had descended into damaging conflicts as a result largely of the allegation that Tajfun considered to be a Serbian DB organisation had infiltrated the Bosnian Serb DB and was undermining its function. This case is about the DB. It's a powerful piece of evidence. If the DB under Mr. Stanisic is not co-operating with the Bosnian Serb DB and is considered to be undermining its function that takes this past assertion and into evidence. We also refer Your Honours to paragraph 111 to 1122 of our closing brief and also Misic transcript 19859 to 19860 and transcript 19883 for further discussions on this point. Turning to slide 10, the Prosecution's assertions concerning Simatovic planning with Dragan to set up paramilitaries in Knin. Slide 10 contains the Prosecution's assertions concerning Simatovic's -- I beg your pardon. Slide 10 contains some of the evidence which we will address to deal with the Prosecution's assertions. First of all, the Prosecution seek to draw massive inference from this document. Despite the fact that Stanisic was only an assistant at the DB at the time, despite the fact as we detail in Annex 1 of our brief that he was being investigated for treason, the Prosecution say if Stanisic -- if Simatovic was planning, so was Stanisic. Secondly, as my learned friends for Mr. Simatovic addressed, the Prosecution have misread the document. This document is further proof that JF-039 was lying about Stanisic when he claimed that he met Stanisic in 1990 and when he claimed that he met Stanisic in January 1991 and the plan was hatched then to create Golubic. The Prosecution claims that Dragan was a integral part of the plan, yet when one reads the document properly, one can see Simatovic did meet Dragan in an April of 1991. But rather than talking about Golubic, supplies to Knin, and so on and so forth, they talked about something quite different. Odd to say the least that a plan had existed for some time to the effect that Stanisic would send Dragan to Knin with Simatovic and other DB instructors but yet the only plan evidenced in this intelligence document is a plan to use Dragan to gather intelligence. The Prosecution appear to accept this document as reliable. More critically, as the document suggests, Simatovic is attempting to find out whether Dragan is transporting weapons through Bosnia which must be to Knin or to the Krajina. It notes on a number of occasions during the conversation, We tried to provoke him regarding any information he might have had -- he might have about the transport of weapons through Bosnia, but in all these cases he acted disinterested with a tendency to dismiss the subject. Very strange indeed. According to JF-039, Simatovic on behalf of Milosevic and Stanisic had been supplying weapons to Knin for eight months. Presumably Dragan, days before he went to Knin, would have been in this informational loop. After all, this was a plan to create paramilitary forces which required weapons for Captain Dragan's Golubic camp, and yet conversely the DB appears to be concerned about Dragan supplying weapons through Bosnia. A curious lack of co-ordination for the Prosecution's elaborate DB plan. The Prosecution today said that while Babic may not have known and that his testimony: "Reveals that when he met Milosevic in March of 1991, it became apparent that Milosevic, Bogdanovic and Stanisic had already been involved in sending weapons to Krajina without Babic's knowledge." But an examination of the relevant exhibit, P1878, page 153 to 154, Babic testimony, shows that what Babic was unaware of was 500 pieces of weapons which had been sent to Banija, not the Serbian MUP trucks, not the Stanisic co-ordination, not thousands of pieces of weapons which the Prosecution case alleges, but 500 weapons to Banija and no Stanisic in that equation. This document, and I'm embarrassed to say, we hadn't noticed the significance of this document, but this may well be the most pivotal document in this whole scenario. If we can turn to slide 11, please. And it deals with an assertion, just moving on to another subject, the priority that the JATD was given in terms of staffing. The Prosecution asserted at T-20202 that the JATD's priority in terms of staffing suggested and showed what an influential and powerful man Mr. Stanisic was and how Milosevic gave him, the DB, priority in terms of resources. Slide 11 contextualises that assertion. Rather than it seems the JATD being an elite force prioritised, it appears to have been an organisation that many employees departed from. Your Honours will also note that this alleged killing machine engaged in extensive combat activities, according to the logic of the Prosecution case, only records that in 1995 four people died.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The same applies to an error I made yesterday concerning JF-032 and my confusion between Bogunovic and Bogdanovic, but the Prosecution again failed to deal with the material issue. Neither of the witnesses, Bogunovic or JF-029 who could be expected to have known about Stanisic screaming in public about Vukovar and then arranging and planning the Vukovar operations confirmed that to be true. The Prosecution presumably asked them and they didn't know. Moving on to slide 13, and I want to deal very briefly with the Prosecution's changing account to Stanisic's alleged command of Arkan. As we understood the Prosecution case from the outset of this trial, and that has been maintained throughout until two days ago, Stanisic was Arkan's direct commander, and as slide 13 shows, taken from the Prosecution's closing, that case has shifted. Now they want Your Honours to accept, having failed to produce a single piece of evidence of Stanisic meeting or communicating with Arkan throughout the whole indictment period, that his liability can rest on the fact that Stanisic knew what was happening in SBWS, that Arkan and Badza co-operated closely, and that Stanisic co-operated with other JCE members and that Stanisic was in charge of Kostic and Kojic. A very different case indeed from that we started off with and have had to struggle with for the last three years. A classic case, we submit, of moulding the case, a classic case of insufficiency of evidence, and a textbook example of attempting to attribute guilt by association. It I can now turn to Trnovo. Slide 14 contains a summary of the steps, we submit, the Prosecution must take to make a finding or establish a finding with regard to the killing of these unfortunate victims. We hope Your Honours will find it useful. It's to show the impoverishment of the position that an association with Kojic or an employment relationship with Kojic is sufficient to show that these security men of Medic's were under Stanisic's control. The Prosecution rely upon Kovac, who is only one of two witnesses, JF-029, being the other, who claim Mijovic was in command at the time. As Your Honours will see in the third column, JF-029 conceded that he was not certain on a different occasion. By the time he arrived in this courtroom, his version was somewhat different. With regard to Kovac, the Prosecution accept he needs corroboration. I think yesterday I referred to Kovacevic by mistake, but I was referring to Kovac. We submit that the problem of Kovac, rightly identified by the Prosecution, extends to Mladic and all evidence from the RS senior leadership. Slide 15 sums up further evidence of the unreliability of Kovac and Mladic as well as providing further evidence of the lack of concerted action of the Serbian DB as an institution and the Bosnian Serb leadership. Slides 16 sums up the steps that the Prosecution must take to establish Mr. Stanisic's liability for Arkan's men, including his alleged financing of the Sanski Most operation. Your Honours will note that the Prosecution have only identified eight of 3- to 400 of Arkan's men being paid per diems. This does not suggest Stanisic's support or the DB's institutional support. On the contrary, it must show that these payments are more personal. And so to conclude, I think well within time, I hope, as with that issue, the issues we've tried to outline in our closing brief and the approach we've tried to take, which is to examine the minutia of the evidence, to strip away assertion and to look far from collective responsibility and to approach individual responsibility, the Prosecution's attempt to turn this trial into a morality play must fail. Motive is not intent. Whatever Stanisic's motives, whether he co-operated with foreign powers to avoid their intelligence services undermining his own, whatever his motives were in relation to a number of acts, many of which are in our brief but are in the annex which deals with mens rea and mitigation, his intent is what this trial is about. And whatever the Prosecution say belatedly concerning his interaction with foreign powers, that assistance was valuable. It impacts on his intent. To assist foreign powers to look for -- could we go into private for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as for the belated suggestion that Mr. Stanisic had turned his undoubted character to assisting, we say this: One man can only do so much. It's difficult to point to any of the Serb leadership who did what he did. We submit that should be the framework for Your Honours' consideration. We're grateful to Your Honours for the time, and we leave the case in your capable hands, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be very brief, and I will address only some of the remarks presented by Ms. Marcus. On page 47 of today's LiveNote, our learned friend says concerning our closing remarks that it is simply unbelievable when you see the video from the ceremony in Kula for someone to hug a person he claims he had no contact with ever. The Defence never claimed in these proceedings that there had been no contacts between Captain Dragan and Franko Simatovic. A lot of evidence has been led in this trial, and the Defence accepts it, that Captain Dragan and Mr. Simatovic had at least two months when they were in Krajina together in the area of Knin and Golubic in 1991. What the Defence denied in its closing remarks is the nature of that relationship. Franko Simatovic and Captain Dragan never had the relationship of members of a joint criminal enterprise who worked together in pursuit of a certain goal. I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the final trial brief of this Defence, paragraph 353, and I shall quote from it. From the document we analysed in the said paragraph, it is abundantly clear that Captain Dragan, in September 1991, upon returning from Knin -- could we just briefly go into private session for me to mention a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Now when we are very comfortable with time, I am in a hurry and it's obvious that we will conclude even before time. The next thing my learned friend cites is Exhibit P693 as the only intercept involving Radovan Karadzic, and from this intercept my learned friend makes the miraculous conclusion that Radovan Karadzic and Simatovic knew each other, they were close, and they were working on a joint project. I will agree that Radovan Karadzic and Franko Simatovic knew each other. From what and how does my learned friend draw the conclusion that they were close? I kindly ask the Trial Chamber again to look at this intercept carefully, P693, and analyse it from beginning to end. It is also possible and desirable to analyse the B/C/S version. What is really important and obvious is that Franko Simatovic is addressing Radovan Karadzic as Mr. Karadzic. They are not on first-name terms. What is important is that when Kertes is passing the receiver to Simatovic, Radovan Karadzic asks, "Who is this?" He doesn't recognise the voice. It certainly casts no less than a reasonable doubt on the assertion that they were close. I would appreciate it if I could get an explanation from my learned friend how and where she reads from the intercept that they were working on a common project. That is really not evident from the conversation. The fact that the Prosecution believes that acquaintanceship is a sufficient test for proving that somebody's involved in a joint criminal enterprise, then the Defence is simply defenseless. My learned friend also mentioned a meeting related to the Operation Udar that Ratko Mladic noted in his diary. My colleague Mr. Petrovic spoke about that in his closing remarks, and we have dealt with a lot of evidence and analysis concerning this in our final trial brief. My question is: What does the presence of Franko Simatovic, who does not contribute to the discussion at that meeting at all mean, and how does it incriminate him or indicate that he was involved in some planning or operation of the VJ? Is it really strange that a certain time after a lot of shells landed in the area of Bajina Basta and the Republic of Serbia that an intelligence officer of the state security sector of the Republic of Serbia has come to familiarise himself with the situation, to assess how serious the threat is to the territory of Serbia and the state of Serbia? It is quite clear from that entry that he was not making any suggestions, that he was not participating in the planning of any actions or operations, and, indeed, that he did not say a word. Isn't it logical and normal to any reasonable trier of fact that an intelligence agent of the State Security Service is displaying interest in a situation that could pose a threat to his state? Is that really evidence of a joint criminal enterprise, his presence at that meeting? The only meeting, I repeat. We have put forward a wealth of evidence that explained the entire Operation Udar, who planned, what they planned. My learned friend also adds concerning this operation that Franko Simatovic together with the Red Berets participated in these operations around Bajina Basta. I kindly ask you to move into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, and towards the very end my learned friend responded also to the five signatures on over 50 pay lists for per diems. Perhaps we and the Prosecution did not really understand one another well. It doesn't matter whether somebody in the hierarchy above or below somebody signs for another person, although it is unusual for a superior to sign for a subordinate. This is about something else. My colleague Mr. Petrovic asked the Trial Chamber to consider why in an internal document from 1994 and 1995, a document addressed to the 8th Administration of the same State Security Service made in realtime, why would it be a problem to write on those five pay lists "Commander Franko Simatovic" and for Simatovic to sign that? The only realistic conclusion is that's because Franko Simatovic was not commander of that unit. Why do we see deputy commander Radonjic? We explained through numerous evidence, including the job staff specification which shows that the commander of the unit did not exist that Radonjic as deputy commander was the highest in rank. We would like to recall that it was a special organisational unit in the State Security Service. When Simatovic signed for Radonjic, he was a special advisor in the state security sector. And it was precisely because it was not the same organisational unit Franko Simatovic, a special advisor, signs for the deputy commander, not because one of them was superior to the other. I repeat again, why would it have been a problem to write in a 10-page pay list "Commander of the unit Franko Simatovic" if that had been the case? At that time there was absolutely no indication that there would be any proceedings before this court. It was an internal document of the State Security Service. Your Honours, I ask you kindly to consider all the arguments provided in our final trial brief and in our closing remarks and our response to the rebuttal of the Prosecution. Thank you very much for the time you granted us and for listening to our remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just one point to clarify something Your Honours asked during our presentation. On page 31, relating to our final brief, pages 1058 and 1059, you should understand that our Defence was dealing with the alleged planning of the Operation Udar. In those paragraphs you will find our position concerning the planning of that operation. That is a clarification of what we have said in our closing remarks today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that especially in 1059, paragraph 1059, that it was about planning and preparation. I raised the matter because the word "Udar" was not in any language referred to in those paragraphs and neither in the preceding paragraph, but thank you for your clarification. Before we conclude, Mr. Bakrac, P693, you asked our specific attention for the original version which of course we have some difficulties in reading where in the telephone conversation between Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Karadzic you said Mr. Karadzic was addressed as Mister. Now, what we find in the translation is that he is twice addressed as Doctor. Do you intend to say the translation is wrong? Then we should ask for a review of the translation, or were you referring to the use at two occasions of the word Dr., or is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters say something before Mr. Bakrac replies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. The interpreters asked whether they could say something before you respond to what I just asked. The interpreters have an opportunity to -- to say whatever they want to say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we interpreted it as "Mr." to indicate that they were not on first-name terms. The word used by Mr. Bakrac was, in fact, that they were addressing each other as "vi," which is the equivalent of "vous" in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is the use of the more polite form, if I could say it. In English it's very difficult to explain. In the French you would say that they were "vous voyez," and not -- and not "tu tries." That is meaning the plural form and not the singular form which is used in some languages as an expression of respect and distance rather than being closer to other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that I -- what I'm going to say will have no probative value whatsoever but in the Serbian language when you don't know somebody well, you also use "vous." When you are closer with somebody, you would address them as "ti," like "tu" in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the record, of course, the Chamber will consider these observations in the context of the entirety of the conversation. Then this having been clarified, if the parties agree on the use of this form in the language, I don't think that we have to do anything with it. Then this then concludes the closing arguments of the parties. Now, there are still a few pending matters which in all likelihood would not require any further hearing. Of course, that can be different, you never know, but as far as we can foresee now there will be no further hearings. The Chamber would like to express its appreciation, appreciation for the often very practical and the very co-operative attitude the parties have shown, especially when the Chamber asked for the assistance of the parties. And I can assure you that all three Judges are convinced that the parties play a vital role in this kind of proceedings. Therefore, we adjourn, as it is said in latin sine die, without a new date. It may well be that after we have dealt with some other matters that we will issue a Scheduling Order indicating when we will deliver judgement. Judgement will be delivered in due course. We stand adjourned sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.45 p.m.
